figures.title: The plant is assets joined by couplings
figures.caption: Each coupling links a port on one asset to a port on another and carries one kind of energy. This plant has 11 assets, 21 ports and 13 couplings.

figures.title: Every asset is an energy transfer function
figures.caption: Each asset has five ports, one per kind of energy: mechanical, fluid, thermal, electrical and chemical. Some ports are unused. Inside the asset, energy changes from one kind to another; between assets, it travels along couplings.

figures.title: The simplest view is every asset against every other
figures.caption: Allowing every port of every asset to couple to every port of every other gives about 25N² possible links, or 2.5 billion for 10,000 assets.

figures.title: Most of that is zeros, and the rest is linear
figures.caption: A real plant has only a few couplings per asset, so the math is a sparse linear system that one CPU core solves quickly; our benchmark ran about 20 ms per update at 10,000 assets on one core. It ran on the CPU only. No GPU was tested. The cost rises sharply when the plant is tightly meshed, to 11.6 s per update at 100,000 assets, or when every vibration cycle is simulated in time.

figures.title: Envelopes from coupling strength, tested against random groupings
figures.caption: We group the assets into envelopes found from how strongly they exchange energy, and test them as a structure for sensing and for reading the plant, against random groupings of the same sizes. In the v1 toy plant the 4 envelopes were set by function, and 5 of 13 couplings cross a boundary. The v2 plant (32 assets) finds envelopes from coupling strength (see Results).

figures.title: Each envelope becomes one asset
figures.caption: Each envelope folds into one block, so the plant-level solve only has to handle the blocks and the couplings between them. The block ports are the ends of the 5 boundary couplings. The study below uses only the power on those couplings for the reduced model, and every port for the full model.
